Jesus is God, we said, in our own way of speaking [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our sage used a chain of Scripture's own names, not a philosopher's definition [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. The Persian sage wrote in Demonstration XVII: [[quote:syr.quote.aphrahat-sure-thing]]

Our poet confesses the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[syr.dw.jesus]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Asked about the Trinity, we answered from our font [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer received the Holy Spirit [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]].

Then we guarded the mystery [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because what God is, is better sung than dissected [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our tradition remembers that our own bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[syr.story.jacob-nicaea]] [[as:paraphrase]]. No account of what he said or did at the council survives [[syr.story.jacob-nicaea]] [[as:paraphrase]]. Our native tongue for the faith was praise [[syr.dw.was-jesus-god]] [[as:paraphrase]].
